commentary.label: Commentator's view
commentary.note: Humility is not praising oneself; lack of pretence is not displaying one's own virtue; non-violence is not harming beings; patience is staying unmoved when wronged.

commentary.label: Commentator's view
commentary.note: Humility is not looking down on the excellent; lack of pretence is not doing good for fame; non-violence is not harming by word, thought or deed; patience is a mind unchanged even when harmed by others.

commentary.label: Commentator's view
commentary.note: Pretence is putting on a show of greatness while knowing one's own smallness.

commentary.label: Commentator's view
commentary.note: Truth is saying what is so, without unkind falsehood; freedom from anger is calming anger that arises when one is abused or struck; not slandering is not exposing others' faults.

commentary.label: Commentator's view
commentary.note: Freedom from anger is having no change of mind that leads to harming others; compassion is being unable to bear the suffering of any being; renunciation is letting go of possessions that work against one's true good.

commentary.label: Commentator's view
commentary.note: Slander is telling a king or others of faults in order to bring trouble on someone; steadiness is not being fickle.

example.label: Historical example
example.title: Gandhi reads the Gita as non-attachment and inner struggle
example.event: M. K. Gandhi translated and commented on the Gita in Gujarati as 'Anasaktiyoga' (the yoga of non-attachment, 1929), reading the battlefield as the inner struggle between good and evil and making detachment from the fruits of action central to daily life, including his commitment to non-violence.
example.source: M. K. Gandhi, Anasaktiyoga (Ahmedabad: Navajivan, 1929). Not yet in the library; summary to be checked against a public-domain edition before review.
example.lesson: A text set on a battlefield was read by a leader of non-violent resistance as a guide to inner discipline and non-violence.
example.limits: Gandhi's allegorical reading differs from the literal setting, and from other interpreters such as Tilak.

challenge.label: Viveka's application
challenge.name: Weigh consequences, harm and your own capacity
challenge.text: If your conscience leans the other way, here is the other view: Weigh consequences, harm and your own capacity. Action begun without regard for its consequences, the loss it causes, harm to others or one's own capacity comes from delusion.

source.label: Source text
source.english: Action undertaken out of delusion, without regard to consequences, loss, harm to others, or one's own capacity, is called tamasic.

challenge.when_the_recommendation_misleads: It is used to tell someone they may not defend themselves or leave a violent situation.
